li.a: PalQuest, Institute for Palestine Studies: Lydda, 9-13 July 1948 (archived copy)
The New York Times, 23 October 1979: Israel Bars Rabin From Relating '48 Eviction of Arabs (archived copy)
Negotiations Affairs Department (NAD): The Massacres of Lydd (Lod) and Ramle During the 1948 Nakba
Al Jazeera: Yousef Munayyer, "It is beautiful... not a single Arab to be seen"

content.p: In the second week of July 1948, in the pause between the first and second truces of the first Arab-Israeli war, Israeli forces took the Palestinian towns of Lydda and Ramle and sent most of their people away. Lydda, east of Tel Aviv, had a railway station and an international airport. Over about four days it was bombed from the air and stormed, and its men were ordered to assemble at mosques and churches; killing broke out on 12 July, and on 13 July the town was cleared. On 13 July a column of tens of thousands of people walked east into the hills in the July heat.

Almost everything about it is argued over: the number who were expelled, the number who were killed, who gave the order, and whether it was a military necessity, an improvised response or part of a policy. This account sets out what the opened sources say and who says it. The sources consulted agree that the two cities fell and that most of their residents left in these days. The commanders faced a question that Yitzhak Rabin later wrote about in terms he was not allowed to publish.
content.h2: Two cities on the road to Jerusalem
content.p: The Palestine Studies encyclopedia (PalQuest) describes Lydda and Ramla as twin cities about three kilometres apart. Lydda held 18,250 people in 1946, according to that source, with no Jews among them; it was known for its olive and sesame oil presses and a Monday market that served the villages around it. Under the UN Partition Plan of November 1947 both towns were to be part of the Arab state.

By July 1948 they were crowded. PalQuest says Jaffa and nearby villages fell between late April and mid-May and that thousands of evicted people sought refuge in Lydda. The commentator Yousef Munayyer writes that Lydda's population of some 20,000 had swelled to 50,000. The Jordanian army company posted between the two cities pulled back when the Israelis attacked, according to PalQuest, and the town's own defenders had little ammunition.

The Israeli aim, as PalQuest puts it, was to relieve pressure on besieged Jerusalem by securing the Tel Aviv to Jerusalem highway, which meant taking Lydda, Ramla, Latrun and the high ground towards Ramallah. Several plans existed. The one adopted was Operation Dani, launched on the night of 9 to 10 July from the Ben Shemen settlement. The New Yorker calls the wider plan Operation Larlar and describes the commander at the headquarters at Yazur as General Yigal Allon, with Rabin as operations officer. The Negotiations Affairs Department (NAD) says the aims also included expanding Israeli territory beyond the lines of the Partition Plan.

NAD says the Israeli air force began bombing Lydda on 10 July and that on 11 July raids on both towns came as people broke their Ramadan fast. PalQuest, which gives no dates for the raids, also describes bombing at that hour; it says dozens were killed and wounded and the hospital overflowed. On the morning of 11 July, the same source says, aircraft dropped leaflets telling Lydda to surrender and leave. The New Yorker says that on 10 and 11 July the 8th Brigade took the northern part of the valley and the airport, and the Yiftach Brigade the southern villages. On 11 July, he writes, in the late afternoon the 89th Battalion under Moshe Dayan drove into the city in armoured vehicles. In an assault he times at forty-seven minutes, he says, dozens of people died by gunfire, among them women, children and the elderly, and the battalion lost nine men.

By the evening, according to The New Yorker, soldiers held the city centre and had confined thousands of civilians in the Great Mosque. PalQuest says Lydda never formally surrendered, though the Israelis took full control on 12 July, imposed a curfew and ordered the men of the town to assemble at the Great Mosque, the Dahmash Mosque and the churches.

The essay's account of the military governor, Shmarya Gutman, which draws on its author's interviews with him, says the Great Mosque was packed by nightfall, with no food, water or room to sit. It says he released the elderly at midnight, then flour-mill owners and bakers, and the next day the children.

What happened next on 12 July is told differently by different authors. The New Yorker, citing the historian Benny Morris for the arrival of two Jordanian armoured vehicles, writes that some Palestinians fired on Israeli soldiers near a small mosque. In its telling the brigade commander gave the order to open fire, some soldiers threw grenades into houses, and one fired an anti-tank shell into the small mosque. It writes that two hundred and fifty Palestinians were killed in thirty minutes. It says that Gutman, during negotiations in the rectory of St George's Church, ordered his men to shoot at any house from which shots came and at anyone breaking the curfew, and that he described the noise as the worst half hour of his life.

PalQuest, which draws on Palestinian testimony, gives a different picture. It says an Israeli woman soldier recounted that a soldier toured the streets with a loudspeaker promising safety to those who stayed in their homes or in the two mosques. The soldiers claimed that snipers were in the houses and threw grenades into them, it says, and people who ran out were shot. A journalist said bodies lay in the streets under the sun for more than ten days. At the Dahmash Mosque, PalQuest gives between 80 and 176 dead and estimates more than 400 dead in the city. NAD cites the Israeli historian Ilan Pappe for 426 killed in a local mosque and nearby streets, and says 176 bodies were found inside the mosque. As PalQuest itself writes, there is no accurate count: its own estimate for the dead in the city and on the march together is close to one thousand.

The 1979 New York Times article names a competing explanation. It says that O Jerusalem by Larry Collins and Dominique Lapierre and Genesis 1948 by Dan Kurzman blamed the eviction from Lod on local residents firing at the Israelis soon after the surrender; it adds that Collins and Lapierre also described "a calculated Israeli policy" to drive Arab residents out.

Rabin's own account of the decision, written for his memoirs, is the best-known record. In the text published by the New York Times in 1979, Rabin says that the fate of the roughly 50,000 civilians of Lod and Ramle was a problem for which there was no precedent. Ben-Gurion, he writes, stayed silent in the discussion at operational headquarters. Outside, Allon repeated his question, "What is to be done with the population?" and Ben-Gurion "waved his hand in a gesture which said, 'Drive them out!'" Rabin writes that after he and Allon held a consultation he agreed it was essential to drive the inhabitants out, and that the people were taken on foot towards the Bet Horon road in the expectation that the Arab Legion would have to look after them.

"'Driving out' is a term with a harsh ring," the manuscript continues. "Psychologically, this was one of the most difficult actions we undertook. The population of Lod did not leave willingly." He wrote that it took force and warning shots to make people march, that some soldiers refused to take part, and that propaganda sessions were needed afterwards to remove the bitterness of youth-movement graduates in the Yiftach Brigade.

The written order is quoted in the same terms by The New Yorker and PalQuest: "The inhabitants of Lydda must be expelled quickly, without regard to age." The New Yorker says Rabin issued it to the Yiftach Brigade. PalQuest says Rabin signed it; the NAD page does not mention the order. PalQuest places the decision on 12 July; The New Yorker places Allon's question and the order in the hours after the shooting.

The brigade commander, Mula Cohen, told the essay's author that there was no explicit expulsion order. "As a state, we do not expel," he said, adding that "some things were said between Ben-Gurion and Allon, but there were no written orders." The essay's own reading is that the training of Palmach officers made orders unnecessary. These two statements, one of a written order and one of none, are not easy to reconcile from the pages consulted.

The New Yorker gives a detailed account of how the surrender of the city turned into departure. Gutman, he writes, met Lydda's leaders three times in the rectory of St George's Church. At the third meeting the dignitaries said they would leave if everyone held in the Great Mosque were released. Gutman told them the prisoners would be free to leave the mosque and Lydda with everyone else. The essay's own view is that the occupation, the killing and psychological pressure had the effect Gutman wanted, so that, in its words, "under the indirect threat of slaughter, Lydda's leaders asked to go."

Gutman told the prisoners they had an hour and a half to leave. The New Yorker says they were forbidden weapons or vehicles and such other possessions as they could carry. By the evening of 13 July, he writes, about thirty-five thousand Palestinians had left Lydda in a long column, marching past Ben Shemen. NAD and PalQuest give about 70,000 for Lydda and Ramle together. Rabin writes that the people of Ramle, having watched, agreed to be evacuated provided it was done by vehicles; buses took them to Latrun, where the Arab Legion took over. Munayyer writes that fewer than a thousand people remained in Lydda.

PalQuest reports that Israeli soldiers gave residents about half an hour to leave and directed them over a rough route towards Ramallah, and that hundreds died of thirst and exhaustion. It reports a small Israeli aircraft flying low over the column. The intelligence officer Shamaria Gottman, quoted by Morris, saw women carrying bundles on their heads and mothers dragging children, with warning shots heard from time to time.

PalQuest quotes three survivors. The artist Ismail Shammut, then eighteen, described an officer who put a gun to his head to make him put down water he had found, and said one of his brothers died of thirst on the march. Reja-e Busailah, then a visually impaired teenager, recalled soldiers with loudspeakers who, in his account, repeated that people had better leave "in order to avoid what happened in the mosque" and who searched people for cash, gold, jewellery and watches. George Habash, later the leader of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine, said a neighbour was shot dead at a checkpoint when he refused a search; he recalled that some people near him called that Ramadan day the Day of Judgment and others called it Hell.

These are memories and are given here as they were given in the source. PalQuest adds that refugees reaching Ramallah were distributed across already overcrowded camps, and that on 2 August 1948 the UN mediator Count Bernadotte visited them there. According to PalQuest, he wrote that he had seen many refugee camps in Europe during the war but never scenes as terrifying as those in Ramallah.
content.h2: Looting, loss and the long argument
content.p: After the exodus, Munayyer writes, Israelis looted the emptied homes and shops. He cites the Israeli historian Tom Segev for 1,800 truckloads of possessions taken from Lydda alone. Munayyer says Ben-Gurion, whom Rabin said ordered the expulsion, expressed shock at the looting. Munayyer then describes how laws declared the property of the displaced "absentee" land, so that, he says, the state came to control 92 per cent of the land.

NAD says Ben-Gurion documented a conversation with Yosef Weitz of the Jewish National Fund on 26 September 1948. In the exchange NAD quotes, cases of refugees from Ramle and Lod reaching Gaza through Ramallah, believing return would be easier from there, were raised, and the answer given was that they had to be "pestered" relentlessly to move on. NAD presents this as evidence of a policy of preventing return.

The account does not appear in either the Hebrew or the American edition of Rabin's memoirs. The New York Times reported on 23 October 1979 that a censorship board of five cabinet ministers, headed by Justice Minister Shmuel Tamir, had forbidden Rabin to include a first-person account. The military censor had cleared the paragraphs, the newspaper wrote. A copy of the manuscript came from the translator Peretz Kidron. "I was puzzled," Rabin said of the deletion, but added that he had to obey the law. The Times noted that his account did not differ markedly from those of authors not subject to censorship, and that Israel was still highly sensitive to the issue.

The arguments left behind concern how to name what happened. PalQuest describes the expulsion as one of the largest acts of ethnic cleansing carried out by the Israelis. Munayyer uses the same term. Cohen, the commander on the ground, rejected the idea of an expulsion order and spoke instead of a belief that both Ben-Gurion and Allon knew an Arab Lydda could not remain by the airport and near Tel Aviv. The essay concludes that Zionism "could not bear" the Arab city of Lydda. The sources consulted do not agree on whether the expulsion was ordered, and the death toll at the mosque remains unsettled.
